cards.meaning: Used to reassure someone that a difficult situation will probably improve or work out.
cards.nuance: This is relaxed and slightly informal, especially in Australian and British English. It can sound dismissive if the person is genuinely worried, so offer practical help when needed.

uses.sentence: The report may look messy right now, but she’ll be right once we’ve checked the figures.
uses.tip: Use it when the outcome really is likely to be fine; otherwise acknowledge the concern.

uses.sentence: Don’t worry about the missed train; she’ll be right soon enough.
uses.tip: It’s reassuring in casual conversation, but it may sound like you are not taking the problem seriously.

uses.sentence: The system should be back online shortly, so she’ll be right.
uses.tip: Best in a message to someone you know well; use a clearer update in a formal email.

origin.summary: Likely developed as a casual reassurance meaning “things will be fine,” especially in Australian and British English. Its exact first use is uncertain.

timeline.text: Similar expressions used the word “right” to mean “fine” or “in order.”
The form “she’ll be right” became established in casual English, particularly in Australia and Britain.
It remains a familiar reassurance, though it can sound dismissive in serious situations.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it when someone needs serious support; it can make their concern feel dismissed.

cards.hint: a warm way to wish someone a good night
cards.meaning: A friendly way to wish someone a deep, peaceful night’s sleep.
cards.nuance: It feels warm and caring, and is especially suitable for friends, family members or close colleagues. It is not normally used in a formal business context.
cards.literal: Sleeping deeply and comfortably, without disturbance.

uses.sentence: You’ve had a long day, so sleep tight after work tonight.
uses.tip: Use it with someone you know well; it may sound too familiar with a new colleague.

uses.sentence: I’ll call you tomorrow, but for now, sleep tight.
uses.tip: Pair it with “good night” or “sweet dreams” for an extra-friendly message.

uses.where: Closing note in a personal email
uses.sentence: Thanks for helping me today. Get some rest and sleep tight.
uses.tip: It works best in a personal sign-off, not in a formal email to a client.

origin.summary: The phrase likely comes from the idea of sleeping soundly and peacefully. It became established as a friendly goodnight wish during the 19th century and later spread into everyday conversation.

timeline.text: The expression developed from the idea of sleeping securely and comfortably through the night.
The phrase began appearing as a wish for a good, peaceful night’s sleep.
It remains a warm, informal way to say goodnight to people you are close to.

cards.pitfall: This is an affectionate phrase, so avoid using it with someone you do not know well or in a highly formal message.

cards.meaning: Used to express confidence that a difficult period will soon improve and better times are ahead.
cards.nuance: It can be encouraging and optimistic, but it may sound like empty reassurance when used without evidence. It is common in conversation, while “I believe better times are ahead” often sounds more measured in professional settings.

uses.where: Team meeting · discussing a slow quarter
uses.sentence: Sales are down now, but with the new campaign launching, the good times are coming.
uses.tip: Pair optimism with a concrete reason or next step.

uses.sentence: Don’t worry, things won’t stay like this forever—the good times are coming.
uses.tip: Use it to comfort someone, but avoid sounding blindly optimistic.

uses.sentence: Although this year has been challenging, the good times are coming as we expand into new markets.
uses.tip: In formal writing, consider explaining what improvement you expect.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from the older expression “a good time is coming,” which predicted that circumstances would improve. The plural form became a general statement that better times were ahead.

timeline.text: A time of enjoyment or prosperity is expected to arrive.
The phrase appears in popular and political speech as a prediction of better conditions.
It remains a common expression of hope, especially during difficult periods.

cards.opposite: the worst is yet to come
cards.pitfall: It can sound unrealistic or overly cheerful when serious problems remain unresolved; offer specific encouragement instead.

cards.meaning: To the greatest extent possible, or as far as someone or something can go.
cards.nuance: It can describe pushing your capacity, effort or resources to their maximum. It may sound encouraging, but it can also suggest that a limit has been reached and should not be pushed further.
cards.literal: Up to the furthest point or boundary.

uses.sentence: We’re stretching the team to the limit with these deadlines.
uses.tip: Use it when capacity or resources are already being pushed hard.

uses.sentence: I pushed myself to the limit trying to beat my best time.
uses.tip: It emphasizes effort and usually implies the activity was very demanding.

uses.where: Performance review · describing a successful launch
uses.sentence: The support team worked to the limit to resolve every urgent issue before the launch.
uses.tip: Pair it with a specific result so it does not sound like vague praise.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from the idea of reaching the furthest boundary of a space, time, resource or physical ability. Its figurative use developed from this literal picture.

timeline.text: Literal sense: reaching the outer boundary or endpoint of something.
Figurative uses appear for maximum effort, capacity and physical endurance.
Common in workplace, sport and everyday speech for describing the maximum someone or something can handle.

cards.pitfall: “To the limit” can imply that no more effort or resources are available, so explain what is already at capacity.

cards.term: too much of a good thing
cards.meaning: Something enjoyable or beneficial has become excessive and is no longer welcome.
cards.nuance: The phrase often has a light, humorous tone, but it can also suggest that a situation is becoming difficult to manage.

uses.where: Planning a full week of events
uses.sentence: Four team socials in one week is too much of a good thing.
uses.highlight: too much of a good thing
uses.tip: Use it gently when extra activities are becoming tiring rather than harmful.

uses.where: Choosing a restaurant for a large group
uses.sentence: We already booked the party room, so having a seven-course dinner is too much of a good thing.
uses.highlight: too much of a good thing
uses.tip: It can add warmth or mild exasperation without sounding seriously annoyed.

uses.sentence: Thank you for offering to help, but too much of a good thing could slow us down.
uses.highlight: too much of a good thing
uses.tip: Pair it with thanks so the reader understands that you appreciate the offer.

origin.summary: The phrase grew from an older English idea that even something good can become bad when taken to excess. Its exact first use is uncertain.

timeline.text: Early English proverbs warned that excess could spoil something beneficial.
Writers began using the wording “too much of a good thing” in its familiar form.
It is a common expression for excess that spoils enjoyment or causes strain.

cards.pitfall: The phrase can sound playful, so avoid it when the excess is causing serious harm or you need a firm warning.

cards.meaning: Accept that some future events are beyond your control and must simply be allowed to happen.
cards.nuance: The phrase can express calm acceptance or resignation. It suits personal and social situations, but it may sound passive when you still have a practical problem to solve.
cards.literal: Whatever is going to happen will happen.

uses.sentence: The client may change the deadline, but whatever will be, will be; we should focus on the work we can control.
uses.tip: Use it after identifying what you can influence, not instead of taking action.

uses.sentence: The picnic might be ruined by rain, but whatever will be, will be—we’ll find something else to do.
uses.tip: It can soften disappointment and help a conversation move on.

uses.sentence: I’m nervous about the interview, but whatever will be, will be, and I’ll give it my best effort.
uses.tip: It works well in personal writing, but avoid it in a formal risk assessment.

origin.summary: This proverb-like wording was already in English use before it became the refrain of the 1956 song “Que Sera, Sera.” The song helped make it a widely recognised expression of acceptance.

timeline.text: A general statement that future events cannot be changed.
The wording appears in collections of sayings and popular expressions.
The refrain “whatever will be, will be” appears in the song “Que Sera, Sera.”
It remains common as a way to express acceptance of uncertainty.

cards.pitfall: The phrase can sound like giving up, so pair it with action when a problem still needs attention.

cards.hint: reassurance that someone can handle it
cards.meaning: A reassuring way to tell someone that they are capable of handling a situation or challenge.
cards.nuance: It sounds encouraging and supportive, but it is informal and may feel unnecessary in a serious or highly professional exchange. It works best with people you know well.

uses.sentence: Don’t worry about the questions; you got this.
uses.tip: Use it with colleagues you know rather than during a formal performance review.

uses.where: Encouraging a friend before an interview
uses.sentence: You know the role inside out, so you got this.
uses.tip: It can feel especially natural among friends who speak casually.

uses.where: Text message before a friend’s exam
uses.sentence: You’ve studied hard, so you got this—good luck!
uses.tip: It is friendly in a message, but too casual for most professional emails.

origin.summary: Likely developed from the older encouragement “you’ve got it,” meaning that someone can cope. The shortened form became common in informal American speech and online communication in the early 21st century.

timeline.text: People used variants such as “you’ve got it” to reassure someone that they could cope.
The shorter “you got this” spreads through casual American speech and online messaging.
It is widely understood as informal encouragement, especially among friends and colleagues.

cards.pitfall: It can sound dismissive if someone is genuinely struggling, so acknowledge their feelings before offering encouragement.
